composition: Nominal composition Fe-30Mn-1.2C-4Al (wt.%), i.e. approximately 30 wt.% Mn, 1.2 wt.% C, 4 wt.% Al, balance Fe. The high Mn and C contents stabilize the fcc austenite so that it tolerates the Al addition without transforming to bcc ferrite; with Al below 5 wt.%, a single austenite phase prevails at room temperature. The 4 wt.% Al addition is an intermediate variant within the Fe-30Mn-1.2C-xAl series, contributing density reduction while keeping the alloy in the single-phase austenitic TWIP (SIMPLEX) regime.
conclusions: The Fe-30Mn-1.2C-4Al sample aged at 450 °C for 1 h is a low-density single-phase austenitic TWIP (SIMPLEX) steel whose intermediate Al content places its mechanical behavior between the embrittling Al-free reference and the aging-strengthened 8 wt.% Al alloy, being only weakly affected by aging. Within the RAP combinatorial framework, this condition contributes to trend screening showing that density-reducing Al additions up to ~4–5 wt.% can be made while retaining a single austenite phase and the TWIP-dominated strain-hardening regime, whereas a stronger aging response requires higher Al and κ-carbide formation.
mechanisms: Al content below 5 wt.% keeps the alloy single-phase fcc austenite, so the TWIP effect prevails as the deformation mechanism: dislocation-based strain hardening at lower loads is followed by mechanical twinning at higher loads, defining the SIMPLEX steel class.
Al additions raise the stacking fault energy, which shifts the overall strain-hardening behavior and the onset of mechanical twinning relative to conventional TWIP steels.

Hot rolling at 1100 °C followed by water quenching and homogenization replaces the coarse as-cast dendritic structure with a fully recrystallized ~20 µm austenite microstructure, while some Mn microsegregation persists.

In the Fe-30Mn-1.2C-xAl series, pronounced aging strengthening is attributed to the formation of nm-sized κ-carbides (L′1₂, approximate stoichiometry (Fe,Mn)₃AlC), an effect that becomes dominant at ~8 wt.% Al; at the intermediate 4 wt.% Al level this precipitation strengthening is much weaker, so aging at 450 °C/1 h only weakly changes the mechanical response.

The intermediate 4 wt.% Al alloy exhibits a much smaller influence of aging on tensile behavior than the ~8 wt.% Al variant, its properties lying between the Al-free alloy (which loses UTS and TE upon aging) and the 8Al alloy (which strengthens upon aging).
microstructure: The aged material is fully recrystallized with a grain size of ~20 µm and retains some Mn microsegregation from solidification. Because the Al content is below 5 wt.%, the sample consists of a single fcc austenite (γ) phase at room temperature, placing it in the single-phase austenitic TWIP (SIMPLEX) steel class. Metallographic inspection found no cracks, pores, or macrosegregations in the final material; the as-cast precursor had a coarse dendritic microstructure that was eliminated by hot rolling and water quenching. No precipitates are reported for this specific 450 °C/1 h condition.
processing: The alloy was melted and cast in a vacuum-induction melting (VIM) furnace under 400 mbar Ar, using a modified system with five stepwise-movable Cu molds successively filled from a 4-kg ingot; after each cast the remaining melt composition was adjusted by charging Al through an air lock. The 10×50×130 mm³ cast blocks were hot rolled at 1100 °C into ~2±0.1 mm thick, ~500 mm long sheets, reheated to 1100 °C and water quenched, then cut perpendicular to the rolling direction into 2×60×55 mm³ segments. Homogenization was performed at 1100 °C for 2 h under Ar followed by water quenching. Aging was conducted at 450 °C for 1 h in air, followed by oil quenching. Scales were removed by low-pressure, fine-grit sandblasting, and test specimens were cut by package spark erosion. This sample is one condition within the 45-condition RAP matrix (five Al contents × nine heat treatments).
properties: Room-temperature tensile testing at an initial strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹ (values are averages of three measurements per material state) yields a yield strength of ~350–450 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of ~460–600 MPa, and a total elongation of ~8–55%. Brinell hardness is ~200 HBW, in line with the nearly flat ~200 HBW level observed across the 0–6 wt.% Al range. Phase characterization by X-ray diffraction was performed on the rolling plane of samples ground to 1 mm thickness, and metallographic cross-sections were prepared perpendicular to the rolling direction. Compared with the Al-free Fe-30Mn-1.2C alloy (which weakens/embrittles on aging) and the Fe-30Mn-1.2C-8Al alloy (which strengthens on aging), the 4 wt.% Al alloy is only very weakly affected by the applied aging treatments.
summary: This sample is the Fe-30Mn-1.2C-4Al (wt.%) intermediate variant of the Fe-30Mn-1.2C-xAl rapid alloy prototyping (RAP) series, processed by vacuum-induction melting, hot rolling, homogenization, and aging at 450 °C for 1 h. As a low-density single-phase austenitic TWIP (SIMPLEX) steel, it was used to screen how a 4 wt.% Al addition modulates the mechanical response to aging relative to the Al-free and 8 wt.% Al counterparts.
unmapped: Al promotes the formation of nanoprecipitates upon aging with L′1₂ structure and approximate stoichiometry (Fe,Mn)₃AlC (κ-carbides), which have a lattice mismatch below 3% with respect to an austenitic Fe-Mn-C matrix and can form cuboidal nanoprecipitates; this is a general statement for the Fe-Mn-Al-C system and is not specifically quantified for the 450 °C/1 h condition of this sample.

This sample was synthesized within the rapid alloy prototyping (RAP) combinatorial approach for trend screening and alloy maturation of Fe-Mn-Al-C low-density TWIP and κ-carbide hardened steels, one of 45 material conditions screened for the Fe-30Mn-1.2C base composition.
